claims.text: Plasma nitriding increases the surface hardness of titanium alloys relative to the untreated state.
Plasma nitriding increases the wear resistance of titanium alloys relative to the untreated state.
Standard titanium alloys in the initial state typically have a native oxide surface.
Plasma nitriding forms a thin, hard TiN layer on the titanium-alloy surface.
Nitrogen diffuses into the titanium substrate during plasma nitriding.
Diffused nitrogen reacts with titanium to form hard titanium nitride compounds.
Titanium nitride formation modifies the near-surface microstructure.
The nitrided near-surface microstructure causes enhanced surface hardness.
The nitrided near-surface microstructure causes reduced wear.
Plasma nitriding is expected to produce roughly 50% higher surface hardness than the untreated alloy.
Plasma nitriding is expected to produce roughly a 30% lower wear rate than the untreated alloy.
The improvements are expected under moderate loads and ambient temperatures representative of aerospace or automotive applications.
The improvements depend on the titanium alloy having sufficient nitrogen uptake.
Very high temperatures may destabilize the TiN phase and limit the improvements.
The magnitude of improvement may vary with alloy composition and plasma-nitriding processing conditions.
The proposed controlled experiment compares standardized plasma-nitrided samples with untreated samples using identical microhardness and wear-test conditions.
Failure to obtain at least a 30% hardness increase together with a wear-rate decrease relative to untreated controls is specified as the falsifying result.
